context:
Maya: Right, Tom, before Dr Lee arrives, shall we go through the equipment for the beach survey?
Tom: Sure. First, the drone. I tried it on Tuesday and the battery only lasted about eight minutes, which is hopeless for mapping the whole bay.
Maya: Eight? I thought it was twenty. Oh, but you were flying into the wind. Still, yes, that's a problem.
Tom: The GPS unit is fine, but we have to reserve it through the department office, and they need a week's notice. So we should book it today.
Maya: Okay. What about the measuring poles?
Tom: I counted six, which is what we need. Hold on, no, the top section of one has snapped off, so effectively one is missing.
Maya: Right, I'll tell the technician. And the tablet for recording data?
Tom: The tablet itself is lovely, but the mapping app is really complicated. I spent an hour just working out how to enter a location.
Maya: Hmm, we'll need a tutorial then. And the camera?
Tom: It's waterproof, so the sea spray won't hurt it. The trouble is that it's incredibly heavy. My arm ached after ten minutes.
Dr Lee: Good morning, both. Sorry I'm late. I've read your proposal. Let's start with the aims. I was going to suggest changes, but on reflection they're perfectly clear, so leave them as they are.
Maya: Great.
Dr Lee: The background reading is quite long, though that's not really the issue. Most of your sources are from the nineties and the field has moved on, so find some recent studies.
Tom: We'll do that.
Dr Lee: The timetable worries me. You've planned to survey the cliffs in January, but the access road is usually closed then. Those dates just aren't realistic.
Maya: Oh, we hadn't thought of that.
Dr Lee: Next, the budget. The figures add up, but you haven't included travel. The minibus alone will cost a fair amount, so add that line. Finally, the risk assessment. It's thorough, but nothing can go ahead until the university safety officer has signed it, and she's only in on Thursdays.
Tom: Right. Now, I've been looking at last year's data for each site. At the north cliff, the retreat is about two metres a year, and it was under one a few years ago, so it's definitely accelerating.
Maya: I thought it had slowed down. Oh, no, I was reading the wrong column. You're right.
Tom: The harbour wall is the one place where the loss is tiny, because of the barrier they installed last year.
Maya: The dunes are interesting. Most of the loss happens during storms. Between storms the dunes actually grow a little.
Dr Lee: The river mouth is harder. I expected a pattern, but the measurements jump around, up one season and down the next, so we can't say anything definite.
Tom: And the caravan park? The cliff there is retreating fast, but I think that's because of the new car park they built behind it, which changed how rainwater drains.
Dr Lee: Hmm, could be. Worth checking. So let's plan next week. On Monday, why not pick up the GPS unit? It's free that day if you ring the office today.
Maya: Fine. On Tuesday there's a tutorial for the mapping software, so Tom and I will go to that.
Tom: I could buy spare batteries on Tuesday too, but the shop's closed, so I'll leave that.
Maya: Wednesday we'll revise the timetable, once we know the dates for the road.
Tom: The safety officer's in on Thursday morning, so we'll get the form signed then.
Dr Lee: Good. In the afternoon you'll have time to visit the north cliff and check the access, so do that.
Maya: And on Friday I'll email the residents' group about the caravan park.

title: Food Waste in the Canteen
context:
Priya: Okay, Jack, let's start with why each food gets thrown away in the canteen. I spoke to the kitchen manager yesterday.
Jack: Great. I assumed bread would be the big one, because of the size of the loaves.
Priya: Actually, it isn't the size. The bread goes stale by the evening and they can't sell it the next day.
Jack: Right. And rice?
Priya: They cook it in enormous batches at noon, even when only half the tables are taken, so loads is left over.
Jack: I thought they reheated it for the next day.
Priya: No, health rules forbid that. Now, salad. I expected the cooks to be at fault, but it's the customers. They pick out the tomatoes or onions and leave the rest, and the whole bowl goes in the bin.
Jack: Typical. What about soup?
Priya: Anything unsold at the end of the day is thrown away. The kitchen says it can't be kept overnight. And fruit is the odd one. Staff don't buy too much, they just leave it in the storeroom until it goes soft, because nobody checks the stock.
Dr Okafor: Hello, both. Tell me about your data. Let's start with the kitchen records.
Priya: We have them for the whole year.
Dr Okafor: Useful, but staff only log what they remember to write down, so there are gaps. I wouldn't rely on them alone.
Jack: We also weighed the bins ourselves for a week.
Dr Okafor: That's your strongest evidence, because it's direct measurement.
Jack: Should we repeat it in another month?
Dr Okafor: I did wonder, but no, one week is enough. What about the student survey?
Priya: Two hundred replies.
Dr Okafor: People tend to overstate how much food they waste, so the figures may make the problem look bigger than it is. And the chef interviews?
Jack: We've done six.
Dr Okafor: Lovely, but transcribing and coding them takes ages, so choose three. As for the supplier invoices, I would love to see them, but the catering company won't let you publish any figures. They're confidential.
Jack: Now our ideas. Smaller plates first. I worry students will just ignore them and go back for more.
Priya: Maybe, but a university in Leeds introduced them and cut waste by a fifth, so that's our best-supported idea.
Jack: Fair enough. Then there's the app that offers cheap food at closing time. I love it, but the developer wants thousands of pounds, which we simply don't have.
Priya: Yes, too expensive. Compost bins, though, we could set up straight away. The porters already have spare containers.
Jack: Brilliant. What about booking meals the day before?
Priya: Apparently they tried that three years ago, nobody used it, and it was dropped.
Jack: Ah. And donating leftovers to a charity?
Priya: It's a lovely idea, but we can't do anything until the catering manager agrees, because of food safety.
Dr Okafor: Let's finish by planning your presentation.
Priya: My first slide is crowded. I've got two whole paragraphs on it, so I'll cut that down.
Jack: The graphs look good on screen, but the numbers on the axes are tiny. People at the back won't see them.
Priya: I'll make them bigger. The video clip is from a television documentary, so I need to ask for permission before we show it.
Jack: I was worried the file wouldn't open on the department computers, but I converted it yesterday, so that's fine.
Dr Okafor: Good. What about your recommendations section?
Priya: We haven't practised it yet. We only wrote it last night.
Dr Okafor: Then rehearse it twice. And leave time for questions. Last year's group had twenty minutes of discussion and ran well over.
Jack: Understood. We'll keep it tight.

title: Does Noise Affect Concentration?
context:
Hannah: Thanks for running the pilot, Ravi. I know it took you all afternoon. How did it go?
Ravi: Mixed. We only needed twelve people for the pilot, but just five replied to our email. I think the subject line was boring.
Hannah: Ah. And the room? I booked the quiet lab.
Ravi: Someone else was already in there when we arrived, so we had to move to the seminar room.
Hannah: Annoying. And the questionnaire?
Ravi: Question six confused everyone. Half of them asked what moderately distracted meant.
Hannah: Okay, I'll reword it. What about the consent forms?
Ravi: Three people forgot to sign theirs and left before I noticed.
Hannah: Oh no. And the timer software?
Ravi: It crashed halfway through twice, so I had to restart the whole session. People turning up late wasn't a problem, though. Everyone was on time.
Hannah: Good. Let's see what Dr Chen thinks of the design.
Dr Chen: I've read it. Participants first. You plan twenty. That's too few for the effect you want, so I'd go for forty.
Hannah: Forty? We'd run out of time.
Dr Chen: Thirty-five is workable, but aim for forty. Now the noise. You're using pop music, but people differ in taste, which muddies the results. Use recordings of traffic instead.
Ravi: And the written summaries are graded by me.
Dr Chen: Since you know which condition each person was in, you could be biased. Ask a second marker to look at them too. Also, you only have noisy conditions. Add a silent one so you can compare.
Hannah: Should we pay the participants?
Dr Chen: Not necessary. Course credit is enough. One last thing. The task is twenty minutes long. That's tiring, and people will make mistakes because of fatigue, not noise. Ten minutes is plenty.
Ravi: Right, ten minutes.
Hannah: Now, analysis. I suggest the spreadsheet. We all know it already, so no training is needed.
Ravi: True. But the statistical package can cope with big datasets, and ours could reach hundreds of rows, so that's the sensible choice if the numbers grow.
Hannah: Is it on the lab computers?
Ravi: No, sadly. We'd have to install it on our laptops.
Hannah: Okay. What about the online calculator some people use?
Ravi: It costs nothing, which is attractive, but I wouldn't use it for the final analysis.
Hannah: And doing it by hand?
Ravi: Slow, but you'd get a very precise answer because you check every step. I'd keep that as a check. Then there's the chart app. It makes the graphs for you automatically, which would save us a whole night.
Dr Chen: Let's agree deadlines. The ethics form has to be with the committee by Friday.
Ravi: I thought it was Monday.
Dr Chen: The committee meets on Monday, so you submit it by Friday. Have all the sessions booked by next Monday. I need your draft report two weeks from now.
Hannah: And the poster? We could do it when the results are ready.
Dr Chen: No, I want a fixed date. It's due at the end of the month. The presentation itself is after the holidays, but finish the slides before they start.
Ravi: Understood. Thank you. It was useful to see everything go wrong before the real experiment.
Dr Chen: Exactly what a pilot is for. Email me if anything is unclear before the weekend.

title: Life in the Rock Pools
context:
Leah: Thanks for lending me your waterproof boots yesterday, by the way. Mine leaked.
Dan: No problem. The rocks were so slippery that I was glad of them.
Leah: Right, Dan, let's pull our field notes together before Dr Patel arrives. Start with the crabs.
Dan: They were fascinating. Every time I came close they scuttled under the nearest rock and refused to come out.
Leah: Same for me. The anemones, then. When the tide went out they looked like blobs of jelly. They had pulled in every tentacle.
Dan: To stop themselves drying out. The limpets hardly moved at all. I marked one with a pen and it travelled only a few centimetres in an hour.
Leah: What about the starfish?
Dan: I only found them in the deepest pool at the far end. And the hermit crabs kept fighting each other over empty shells. I read that shore crabs can change colour, but I never saw it happen.
Dr Patel: Hello, both. Let me look at how you collected your data. Your quadrat counts are fine, they're accurate enough for this kind of survey.
Leah: Good. We took the temperature readings whenever we remembered.
Dr Patel: That's the weakness. Take them at the same time each day, otherwise you can't compare them.
Dan: We wondered whether the photographs were pointless.
Dr Patel: Not at all, they're valuable, but make sure you back them up in more than one place. And the tide times?
Leah: We only noted them twice a day.
Dr Patel: That's too infrequent for a study like this. Check them at least hourly. Finally, your notebook. I couldn't follow it, because every page has a different layout. You need a clear system, with the same headings each time.
Dan: Okay, now the sites. We visited five pools. Pool A was the first one, simply because it's closest to the road. You can get there in two minutes.
Leah: Pool B has by far the greatest variety of species, which is why I want to describe it in detail.
Dan: Pool C was surveyed by last year's group, so we can compare our figures with theirs.
Leah: Pool D is where the school visits happen. It's shallow and safe for children, so we can recommend it for teaching.
Dan: And Pool E is behind the headland, so the oil spill last spring never reached it. That makes it a good clean reference.
Leah: Let's use Pool A as well, though, since it's next to the car park.
Dan: Hmm, I'd skip that reason. Convenience isn't a scientific argument. Closest to the road is fine as a note, though.
Dr Patel: Now, your sources. Textbooks are fine for background, but use them sparingly. Most of your references should be journal articles. They are the main evidence.
Leah: And websites?
Dr Patel: Check carefully who wrote them. If you can't tell, don't use them. If you quote the fishermen you interviewed, ask permission first.
Leah: Should we avoid last year's report altogether?
Dr Patel: No need. You can use it, just cite it in full.
Dr Patel: One more thing. Keep your references in a single list as you write, rather than leaving them until the end. It saves hours.
Dan: Thank you. That's very clear. We will send you a draft by the end of next week.

title: Power for an Island Village
context:
Aisha: I have just come from the library, where I found a report on a similar island in Scotland. It was really useful for the figures.
Ben: Brilliant. We can use it as a comparison later.
Aisha: Okay, Ben, let's compare the energy options for the village before Professor Walker arrives. Solar panels first.
Ben: They'd give plenty of power from May to August, but in winter the output drops badly. So they work best in summer.
Aisha: And the wind turbine? I know you worried about the noise.
Ben: I did, but the latest models are almost silent, so I've dropped that objection. The real risk is the weather. Storms on the island are fierce and could damage the blades.
Aisha: Right. The diesel generator is what they use now.
Ben: And it's costing a fortune. The fuel has to be shipped in, so it's very expensive to run.
Aisha: What about batteries to store the power?
Ben: They're surprisingly simple. Once they're installed they need hardly any maintenance. Finally, the small hydro scheme on the stream. It's a lovely idea, but you can't build anything on the stream without a permit from the environment agency.
Professor Walker: Good afternoon. I like the ambition of the project, but ambition has to be backed by numbers, so I've been through your calculations. Let's start with demand. You've assumed each house uses twenty kilowatt hours a day. That's too high for a village this size. Eight to ten would be more realistic.
Aisha: Oh, I took the figure from a mainland town.
Professor Walker: Exactly. The panel area, though, is about right for the demand you have chosen. No change needed there.
Ben: And the batteries?
Professor Walker: The capacity you propose is too low. If there are three cloudy days in a row, the village would be in darkness. Increase it. The cost estimate is thorough, but present it in a table. It's hard to follow in paragraphs. As for the payback period, ten years sounds optimistic. Go back over those numbers.
Aisha: Will do.
Ben: Now, we've spoken to the community. The older residents were strongly in favour. Several of them remember the blackouts of the nineties.
Aisha: The fishermen worried about the view from the harbour, because the turbine would stand on the headland.
Ben: The café owners were concerned about the cost to them. They think their bills might rise.
Aisha: The teachers at the school wanted more information. They asked for a leaflet to share with parents.
Ben: And the farmers offered to help. One of them has a digger and said he'd lend it for the foundations.
Professor Walker: Excellent. Let's plan the next stages. You'll carry out the feasibility tests next week, while the weather is still calm.
Aisha: And the presentation to the community?
Professor Walker: In the spring. You'll order the parts in the summer, once the funding arrives, and installation will be next autumn, before the storms. We'll review the whole system after a year of use.
Professor Walker: Send me the revised calculations by Thursday and I will read them over the weekend.
Ben: Perfect. We will do that, and thank you for being so clear about what needs changing.

context:
Ibrahim: I finished rereading it last night. The ending still surprised me, even the second time.
Chloe: Me too. I stayed up until two in the morning. Right, before Dr Hughes comes, let's agree what we think of the main characters in Great Expectations. Pip first.
Ibrahim: He changes the most, doesn't he? He starts as a village boy and ends up as someone completely different.
Chloe: Yes. Although I'd say Estella changes more at the end. No, on reflection it's Pip, because the whole book is about his development.
Ibrahim: And Estella?

title: Launching a Reusable Cup Business
context:
Zoe: Marcus, thanks for coming early. I've finished going through the survey results, and I'd like us to agree what each customer group told us.
Marcus: No problem. I printed all two hundred responses, so we can check anything you say. Start with students.
Zoe: Students care about price above everything. They said they'd buy a cup only if it cost less than five pounds.
Marcus: What about office workers? I assumed they'd be our best customers.
Zoe: They like the idea, but most said they forget to bring the cup to the café. So forgetting is the real problem.
Marcus: Tourists?
Zoe: They would happily pay extra for a stylish design, as a souvenir. One woman said she'd pay twenty pounds.
Marcus: That is a useful idea for a special gift range, with the town name printed on the side.
Marcus: Did anyone say they already own one?
Zoe: Lots did, actually, but that wasn't the main point for any particular group. Parents were different. They're worried about hygiene, whether the cup gets washed properly.
Marcus: And retired people?
Zoe: They buy coffee mainly at weekends, when they meet friends. So weekend promotions might work.
Zoe: It is exciting, isn't it? A year ago this was just a joke in the kitchen.
Ms Ferreira: Good afternoon, both. Sorry I am late, the train was delayed. I have read your business plan twice, and it is promising. Let's look at your costings. Materials first.
Zoe: Bamboo fibre, about one pound twenty a cup.
Ms Ferreira: That's higher than I would expect. Most start-ups pay under a pound. Production?
Marcus: We've been quoted fifty pence a cup.
Ms Ferreira: That's lower than I expected, well done. Packaging, then. You've listed a gift box.
Zoe: It's expensive, but the supplier said we could get a cheaper box from a different firm.
Ms Ferreira: Then change supplier. For advertising you've put three thousand pounds. That seems normal for this industry. And delivery. Put it in a separate budget line, because costs vary with distance.
Marcus: We thought insurance wasn't needed yet.
Ms Ferreira: Actually, you do need it, so add that too.
Zoe: Now, where we sell. An online shop would be cheap to run, but it grows slowly because nobody knows us.
Marcus: A market stall earns the most per cup, since there's no middleman, though it's tiring.
Zoe: Cafés might stock them, but only if we agree to supply at least five hundred cups upfront.
Marcus: The university shop would reach thousands of students quickly, which is great.
Zoe: Supermarkets need us to have a special licence, and we've no idea how to get one.
Ms Ferreira: Let's decide who you'll contact this week. The bank first. You will ask about a loan for the first batch.
Marcus: And the supplier, to get a quotation for five hundred cups.
Zoe: The lawyer, to register our brand name before someone else does.
Marcus: The designer, to redo the logo. It looks too childish.
Zoe: And the accountant, to help with tax. We're confused about it.
Ms Ferreira: Will you test the cups at a laboratory?
Marcus: No, we'll test them ourselves in the kitchen.
Ms Ferreira: Fine. Come back to me on Friday and tell me how it went.
Marcus: We will email you a revised budget tomorrow, with the insurance included.

title: Reporting on a Summer Dig
context:
Grace: I still cannot believe how quickly the month went. My knees have only just recovered.
Hamid: Mine too. Okay, before Dr Moreno arrives, let's list what we found in each trench so the report is accurate.
Hamid: Trench A was the best one. We uncovered a long stone wall, nearly four metres of it.
Grace: Trench B was mostly pottery, hundreds of small fragments, but only a few big enough to piece together.
Hamid: I remember Trench C as the one with the glass beads, but no, that was the exhibition in the museum shop. Trench C gave us animal bones, mostly sheep.
Grace: Right. Trench D had the layer of charcoal, which suggests there was once a fire. And Trench E produced the coins. At first I thought they were washers from the machinery, but they're definitely Roman.
Hamid: Good. Here's Dr Moreno.
Dr Moreno: Morning, both. You both look rather tired, but I am told the dig went well. Let's talk about dating. Radiocarbon first. You'll have to send the samples abroad, because no lab here does it any more, and it takes about two months.
Grace: Two months! And tree rings?
Dr Moreno: That's not possible. We found no wood at all, so there's nothing to measure.
Hamid: We could date the pottery ourselves, couldn't we?
Dr Moreno: Yes, the students can do that by comparing the styles with the reference collection. The coins will give you the most precise date, because each one carries the year it was made.
Grace: And the soil layers?
Dr Moreno: They only show which objects are older than others. They give a relative order, not actual years. Radiocarbon may be expensive, but the department has agreed to pay for it, so don't worry about the cost.
Hamid: Now, the difficulties. The heavy rain in the second week stopped us working for seven days.
Grace: Funding was a bigger problem. Halfway through we ran short of money, so we had to give up the plan to open a fifth trench and enlarge the first one instead.
Hamid: The volunteers from the village were a pleasant surprise. They worked all day and even brought sandwiches. They showed us where an old well used to be.
Grace: A neighbour's cows broke through the fence one night and trampled part of Trench B. We lost some of the surface.
Hamid: And then there was the argument with the landowner about where we could park. That took three meetings. Fortunately the broken generator was fixed within an hour.
Dr Moreno: Now, the report itself. Where does everything go?
Grace: Could the site map go on the cover?
Dr Moreno: No, put it in the introduction, so the reader sees it first. The photographs of the trenches belong in the appendix.
Hamid: What about the finds list? It's forty pages long.
Dr Moreno: Then it needs its own booklet. Keep your interpretation in the main text, of course. As for the list of volunteers, put it on the website only. It doesn't need to be in the printed version.
Dr Moreno: I need a full draft by the end of the month, and I would like to see the photographs as soon as they are labelled.
Grace: Perfect. We'll start writing tonight, and Hamid will label the photographs tomorrow.

title: Getting Around the City
context:
Tara: Hi, Leo. Thanks for staying late. I'd like to go through the complaints from our public transport survey one route at a time before we see Dr Singh.
Leo: No problem. I missed the last bus home yesterday, so I feel I understand the complaints better now. Route 12 first.
Tara: The main complaint is overcrowding. In the morning rush people can't even get on the bus.
Leo: Route 34 is different. People there said the buses are often late, sometimes by twenty minutes.
Tara: Yes. And some said that drivers were rude, but only two people, so I'd ignore it. The night bus got a lot of comments about stopping so early. The last one leaves at half past eleven, which is no use if you work in a restaurant.
Leo: The airport express was all about price. Passengers said the fare was too high for a thirty minute trip.
Tara: And finally the tram. People like it, but they complain that the stops are too far apart, especially for older passengers.
Dr Singh: Hello, you two. Sorry to keep you waiting. I have spent the morning reading your report, and it is a good start. I've looked at your methods. Your sample size is good. Four hundred responses is enough for a city this size.
Tara: Thank you.
Dr Singh: The questions are a problem, though. Several are leading. For example, you ask, don't you agree that fares are too high? That pushes people to say yes.
Leo: Oh, we hadn't noticed.
Dr Singh: And you only handed out forms at the central station, so your results are biased towards commuters. You'd have missed students and shoppers. Next, timing. You surveyed on weekdays only, so I'd repeat it at weekends.
Tara: Is the form too complicated?
Dr Singh: No, it's quite clear. Finally, the data entry. I found three mistakes in a sample of twenty rows, so check it again.
Leo: Right. Now, improvements. Tara, I like dedicated bus lanes. They'd cut journey times a lot.
Tara: They're expensive, though.
Dr Singh: Cost isn't the issue. They'd reduce delays, and that's what matters. Contactless payment is already being tested on two routes, as I'm sure you know.
Leo: We didn't. And shelters with seats?
Tara: Mostly for older people, who struggle to stand for a long time at the stops.
Leo: A real-time app showing arrivals is something we could introduce within a few weeks.
Dr Singh: Safe cycle storage at stations is a great idea, but the council must approve it first.
Tara: Okay, now the charts. Chart one shows the age of passengers. The majority are under thirty.
Leo: Chart two, satisfaction by time of day. It drops sharply after eight in the evening.
Tara: Chart three, car ownership. People with cars hardly ever use buses.
Leo: Chart four shows why people are unhappy. Cost comes first.
Tara: And chart five is weekend use, which has been rising each month. I thought few people knew about the app, but sixty per cent do.
Dr Singh: Good. Present it on Tuesday, and keep it to fifteen minutes. The city officials will be there, so speak slowly and avoid jargon.
Leo: We will practise tomorrow. Thanks again for your time.
